transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-05
Time: 15:30 UTC / 11:30 ET
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Dylan Park (Redwood AE), Rina Patel (Redwood SE), Miguel Torres (Cartograph Labs - Head of ML), Aisha Rahman (Platform Eng), Jordan Lee (CTO)
Links shared: https://redwood.company/pilot-runbook (deck), https://sheets.example.com/cartograph-pilot-results (benchmark sheet)

Summary: Quick sync to review last 48h pilot runs; discuss queueing/backpressure spikes observed during mid-run; retune continuous-batching and concurrency targets; agree next steady-state experiments.

00:00:04 - Dylan Park: hey everybody, thanks for makin time, uh quick check that audio's ok?
00:00:09 - Miguel Torres: yeah i hear you, loud and clear
00:00:12 - Aisha Rahman: good here
00:00:15 - Dylan Park: great. goal for today — walk through the latest steady runs you sent yesterday, talk through why we saw that mid-run latency spike at ~+22 minutes, and propose a retune. Rina will run through kernel/queueing theory and then we'll action next runs.

00:01:02 - Rina Patel: cool. quick context — last two runs were with concurrency target 56, continuous-batching enabled default threshold 8ms, prefix caching on, kv cache warmup allowed. you saw throughput around 1.2k tokens/sec for most of the run but then spikes to 4-5s p99 for a few bursts. right?
00:01:24 - Miguel Torres: yes that's what the sheet shows, p50 stable ~120ms, p90 ~380ms, p99 hit 4.8s for a 30s window. we were surprised, we thought KV cache warmup would make it smoother.
00:01:43 - Rina Patel: yeah so two likely culprits — cold KV cache fragmentation on long tail requests and queue head-of-line blocking when a large decode ( > 2k tokens) shows up and steals GPU scheduling slot, plus occasional kernel fallback onto slower path.

00:02:15 - Jordan Lee: when you say kernel fallback, is that like CPU fallback or just slower GPU kernel?
00:02:20 - Rina Patel: mostly slower GPU kernel — the runtime selects a different attention kernel for long sequences; if the batch mixes short and very long sequences, the batch exec path can serialize and increase latency for the whole batch.
00:02:33 - Jordan Lee: mmh ok

00:03:02 - Dylan Park: can you describe how continuous-batching interacts with concurrency targets? like if we bump concurrency higher does that amplify the head-of-line effect?
00:03:13 - Rina Patel: good question. continuous-batching fills batches over a short window. higher concurrency means more in-flight batches; that generally improves throughput and amortizes kernel overhead, but if you have long-tail tokens it can create situations where a slow batch holds up a slot that other requests are waiting on. you can mitigate with queue depth caps per worker and per-session priority.

00:04:01 - Aisha Rahman: are those queue caps something we can change on the hosted side or do we need private deploy? we are in dedicated pilot nodes now right?
00:04:09 - Dylan Park: you're on Dedicated pilot pools — we can adjust node-level queueing and per-route concurrency and we've already got a config toggle for per-session priority and small-request preemption.
00:04:22 - Aisha Rahman: ok cool

00:05:00 - Miguel Torres: just to add, our workload has a bimodal length distribution: 65% under 150 tokens, 30% 150-600, and occasional 5% long-ish >2k tokens. the long ones are important for some merchant analytics but they blow up the p99.
00:05:21 - Rina Patel: that's exactly the case where we recommend a two-tiered routing: small-request fast lane (lower batching window, strict concurrency cap) and large-request lane with higher batching tolerance. also use model-variant with quantized kernels for large runs if you can accept slight quality diff.

00:06:10 - Jordan Lee: interesting. we had been routing everything to same endpoint, didn't think to split. how hard is it to set up two routes?
00:06:17 - Dylan Park: it's a config change in console — you can create route rules by token length or by header flag. we can provide example rules.
00:06:28 - Miguel Torres: can you show the example rules now?
00:06:30 - Dylan Park: yeah, i'll paste the sample later, but Rina i'll let you go through the retune suggestions.

00:06:45 - Rina Patel: sure. propose three quick retunes for next steady-state runs:
00:06:53 - Rina Patel: 1) conservative run: concurrency 48, batching window 6ms, preemption enabled for small requests; 2) aggressive run: concurrency 64, batching window 12ms, KV cache early warmup disabled (observe warmup cost); 3) hybrid run: two-route strategy — small route concurrency 40 batch window 4ms, large route concurrency 12 batch window 20ms.
00:07:23 - Miguel Torres: okay so conservative and hybrid seem safe. aggressive might be risky for us but we'd like to know ceiling.

00:07:40 - Aisha Rahman: what about queue max depth? last run had queues build to 220 requests occasionally — is that too high?
00:07:47 - Rina Patel: 220 is high for per-node queue depth in dedicated mode; we typically keep per-worker queue under 120 to maintain predictable p99s. you can smooth peaks with burst capacity and fallback to compatible smaller model variant when queue depth crosses threshold.

00:08:24 - Miguel Torres: ok, you mentioned fallback — do we get deterministic per-request fallbacks? we want to ensure correctness for those high-value long queries.
00:08:31 - Dylan Park: fallbacks are configurable per-route. you can mark requests as non-fallback via header if you need strong fidelity. otherwise fallback to compatible model variant or different region.

00:09:10 - Jordan Lee: latency vs cost tradeoff — what's the ballpark token cost impact of running concurrency 64 vs 48?
00:09:18 - Rina Patel: depends on batching efficiency. if you increase concurrency and sustain batching, cost per token goes down by kernel amortization. however, if higher concurrency leads to more tail work or fallback to slower kernels, cost can go up. our rough estimate from similar pilots: steady state concurrency 48 yields 0.9x unit cost vs 64 yields 0.75x unit cost provided batching stays efficient. but if you hit serialization you'd see cost spike +20–30%.

00:10:05 - Miguel Torres: great. let's talk about the mid-run spike at ~+22 min in our run. we observed a pattern where p99s hopped when a background reconfiguration job kicked in on the node. could that be causing kernel contention?
00:10:20 - Rina Patel: yes. background maintenance tasks or autoscaler churn can temporarily steal GPU context or memory pages, causing kernels to recompile or reprovision. we recommend pinning pilot nodes (no autoscale) during steady-state tests and disabling admin tasks in window.
00:10:38 - Aisha Rahman: we did have a node reflow around that time — our infra team did a rolling update mistakenly. ok that explains it.

00:11:05 - Dylan Park: good find. mitigation: pin nodes for the 30–60 minute runs, and enable explicit KV-cache priming prior to ramp. Rina, how aggressive should priming be?
00:11:17 - Rina Patel: a 5–10 minute priming pass with representative traffic should get KV hit rates >90%. alternatively, use our prefix prefetch API to load embeddings/past tokens for the common prompts which is faster.

00:12:00 - Miguel Torres: do you have a script for priming?
00:12:04 - Dylan Park: yes, will include a simple curl-based priming script in the retuned runbook.

00:12:30 - Rina Patel: also watch for cross-request batching mixing short and long sequences. small-route separation avoids that. if you can't split by route, enable small-request preemption which evicts small requests into a fast lane when a long job arrives.

00:13:10 - Jordan Lee: what about tokenization differences? we saw small variance depending on model variant; can that affect batching distribution?
00:13:18 - Rina Patel: yep, tokenization can change sequence length profile; recommend normalizing to same tokenizer and feeding length header so router rules remain accurate.

00:13:45 - Miguel Torres: logging — we need better traceability of which request ended up on which kernel path. current logs are ambiguous.
00:13:53 - Rina Patel: we can add a kernel-path tag to the request tracing — it's a small agent update and we'll push it to your pilot tenant; that'll help correlate p99s to kernel churn.

00:14:20 - Aisha Rahman: perfect.

00:14:40 - Dylan Park: ok quick time check — i'll share the three configs you can run. also we noticed in your sheet one run had a big burst at minute 9 when queue depth shot up after a traffic spike from your A/B test. are you able to replay that synthetic pattern?
00:14:58 - Miguel Torres: yes that's reproducible. we run occasional batch ingestion which produces short-term spike. we can include that in the synthetic test.

00:15:26 - Rina Patel: if you're including that spike in the test, please run both with and without lane-splitting so we can measure effectiveness of route separation.

00:16:00 - Miguel Torres: sounds good. question: how will we quantify success? what KPIs do you recommend?
00:16:08 - Rina Patel: core KPIs: p50/p90/p99 latency, sustained throughput (tokens/sec), unit token cost, percentage of requests hitting KV cache, and variance metric (stddev of p99 across 5-minute windows). include failure rate and number of fallbacks per run.

00:17:05 - Jordan Lee: do you have a recommended chart/dashboard?
00:17:09 - Dylan Park: we'll share a Grafana template and the sample spreadsheet with expected columns.

00:17:40 - Miguel Torres: let's pick concrete values to run next: Miguel: run conservative and hybrid first. conservative concurrency 48 and hybrid two-route. we'll do 30-minute steady-state each. if both look stable we'll run aggressive 60-min later.
00:17:58 - Dylan Park: noted. to summarize: conservative (48, batch 6ms), hybrid (small route 40/4ms, large 12/20ms). we'll add queue depth cap 120 for all runs and pin nodes. priming 8 minutes before start.

00:18:28 - Aisha Rahman: question about monitoring — will console show queue depth per-worker in realtime?
00:18:34 - Rina Patel: yes, we expose per-worker queue depth and per-route concurrency metrics. you'll also get trace IDs for any fallback event.

00:19:05 - Miguel Torres: okay i just updated the sheet with the runs we'll kick off tonight. link: https://sheets.example.com/cartograph-pilot-results (we'll add run IDs).

00:19:24 - Dylan Park: great, once you run please paste the run IDs and we'll pull logs and check kernel-path tags.

00:19:50 - Rina Patel: i want to flag one more nuance — continuous-batching window should be tuned to input variance. if your short requests arrive very bursty, a very small window reduces p99 but may reduce batching efficiency. we suggest measuring batching efficiency metric (tokens per kernel call) per run.

00:20:25 - Miguel Torres: makes sense. can you give an example of a metrics formula?
00:20:29 - Rina Patel: sure — batching efficiency = total tokens processed / total kernel invocations over steady window. aim higher is better; we often target >300 tokens/kernel for these models.

00:21:10 - Jordan Lee: are we constrained by memory on dedicated nodes if we increase concurrency? we have 32GB per GPU on pilot nodes.
00:21:18 - Rina Patel: memory constrains how much kv cache and batch size you can hold. concurrency higher increases total in-flight kv and activation memory. we'll check your model size in the runbook and recommend quantization level if necessary.

00:21:48 - Aisha Rahman: speaking of quantization, is there a recommended variant for latency-sensitive large requests?
00:21:54 - Rina Patel: a 4-bit quant variant often gives good speed gains with minimal quality diff on long completions; we'll list the verified model variants in the retuned docs.

00:22:20 - Miguel Torres: ok so timeline — we'll run conserv/hybrid tonight and post by tomorrow morning, then we can reconvene next week. any blockers on your side?

00:22:33 - Dylan Park: none. we'll prepare the retuned runbook and the priming script and push a small tracing tag change (kernel-path). expect artifacts by 2026-10-07.

00:23:05 - Rina Patel: one more thing — there's a small chance we'll ask you to run a 5-minute micro-burst with aggressive concurrency to trigger the head-of-line scenario for debugging; if you can allow that test, it will help us tune preemption.
00:23:20 - Miguel Torres: we can do that in a staging window.

00:23:40 - Dylan Park: ok going to the recap: items and owners in the chat. I'll also send a short one-pager with the three config snippets.

00:24:05 - Aisha Rahman: quick Q — security/compliance: do any of these changes affect audit logs or retention?
00:24:12 - Dylan Park: no, not for retained logs. only change is we add kernel-path tag to trace metadata; we won't change PII or payload retention. full security docs are in the shared drive.

00:24:40 - Miguel Torres: perfect.

00:25:00 - [small pause, typing sounds]
00:25:30 - Jordan Lee: outbound question — we briefly discussed SAM L / SSO last week. unrelated to throughput but timeline for procurement?
00:25:38 - Dylan Park: our procure/legal rep will pick up after pilot sign-off. we'll share standard SAML SSO + SOC2 docs in the same packet.

00:26:05 - Rina Patel: back to tuning — a practical note: when you run these steady-state tests, include a steady synthetic trace generator — it's better than pure replay because it adds micro-variability and makes the test more realistic.
00:26:20 - Miguel Torres: ok we'll adjust our runners.

00:27:00 - Dylan Park: any other technical Qs before we wrap?
00:27:05 - Miguel Torres: only one — is there a simple flag to force small-request preemption?
00:27:11 - Rina Patel: yes: route.preemption.enabled = true; and route.small_request_threshold = 200 tokens. small requests get prioritized.

00:27:45 - Aisha Rahman: will enabling preemption increase cost?
00:27:50 - Rina Patel: negligible change; might slightly increase kernel calls but reduces p99 so net cost per request typically improves.

00:28:20 - Dylan Park: we're at ~28 min — still early but want to align on when to reconvene. suggest a short check next Tuesday if results come in earlier, otherwise weekly sync same slot next Monday.
00:28:33 - Miguel Torres: next Monday works for us.

00:29:00 - [brief cross chatter about timezone]
00:29:30 - Dylan Park: okay final recap in chat now:
00:29:35 - Dylan Park: - Run conservative 30m (C=48, batch 6ms, queue cap 120, pinned nodes, priming 8m)
00:29:45 - Dylan Park: - Run hybrid 30m (small 40/4ms, large 12/20ms)
00:29:52 - Dylan Park: - If both stable, run aggressive 60m (C=64, batch 12ms)
00:29:58 - Dylan Park: - Redwood to send retune runbook, priming script, and kernel-path trace tag (by 2026-10-07)
00:30:10 - Miguel Torres: ok we've got that

00:30:35 - Rina Patel: one final technical callout — when measuring p99, use windowed p99 over 5-minute windows to avoid single outlier influencing decision.
00:30:50 - Miguel Torres: noted

00:31:20 - Jordan Lee: curious — you mentioned early that the continuous-batching window was in ms, right? is there a min granularity?
00:31:27 - Rina Patel: yes it's configured in milliseconds in the route config, minimum 1ms but in practice 3–4ms is the floor due to scheduling jitter.

00:32:05 - Dylan Park: ok any outstanding asks for artifacts?
00:32:09 - Miguel Torres: retuned config + priming script + example route rules + grafana template.
00:32:16 - Dylan Park: will do.

00:33:00 - [short silence]
00:33:30 - Aisha Rahman: one more thought — if we see persistent variance after retune, can we request a micro-profile capture? some way to capture GPU kernel timings per batch?
00:33:42 - Rina Patel: yes, we can enable micro-profiling for short windows; it adds minor overhead but is invaluable. request it on the run IDs and we'll enable.

00:34:10 - Miguel Torres: ok we'll ask if needed.

00:34:45 - Dylan Park: all right, i'm going to post the recap and the action_items now. thanks everyone.
00:34:55 - Miguel Torres: thanks, really helpful
00:35:00 - Jordan Lee: thanks
00:35:03 - Aisha Rahman: thanks

00:41:20 - Miguel Torres: got it
00:43:00 - Dylan Park: ok last administrative note — we'll keep logs for the pilot for 90 days but can extend if you need.
00:44:10 - Miguel Torres: ok good to know
